title: Supreme Court halts contempt case against Punjab's top official over unpaid DA arrears
dek: The court said it did not appreciate 'arm-twisting' and asked Punjab to say how much of its employees' and pensioners' dearness allowance arrears it will pay by 31 March 2027.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Supreme Court on Thursday stayed criminal contempt proceedings against Punjab's Chief Secretary over the state's failure to pay pending dearness allowance (DA) to its employees and pensioners, saying it did not appreciate "arm-twisting" tactics, LiveLaw reported. It asked the state instead to tell the court how much of the arrears it will pay by 31 March 2027.

A bench of Justices B.V. Nagarathna and R. Mahadevan stayed further proceedings in the criminal contempt case pending before the Punjab and Haryana High Court and ordered that no coercive steps be taken in a connected civil contempt case. The bench was told that the state has raised DA from 43% to 53%.

## What the court said

During the hearing, Justice Nagarathna asked the employees' side whether it wanted the High Court's order complied with or the Chief Secretary sent to jail, according to LiveLaw. "Who is going to pay you?" she asked, referring to the summoning of the state's top civil servant. Senior Advocate Devadatt Kamat appeared for the employees; Senior Advocates Vikas Singh, Shadan Farasat and P.S. Patwalia appeared for the state, its officials and the Punjab State Power Corporation Limited (PSPCL).

The matter is listed as Additional Chief Secretary v. Manjeet Singh Randhawa, SLP(C) No. 38661 of 2026, with connected cases. The Supreme Court now has three cases before it: separate appeals by the state and PSPCL against the High Court's main judgment, and the criminal contempt matter.

## How it got here

In August, the Punjab and Haryana High Court dismissed appeals by the state government and PSPCL and held that once Punjab had adopted the Centre's pattern for DA and dearness relief, it was bound to release the instalments that had fallen due and could not put them off indefinitely by pleading financial constraints. It ordered all pending instalments paid by 18 August at the rates paid to All India Services officers in Punjab, with 6% simple interest on late payments, and barred the state from "unproductive expenditures", such as large advertising campaigns, until the dues were cleared.

The Chief Secretary was to file a compliance affidavit by 31 August. The state said it had challenged the judgment in the Supreme Court on 1 September. On 9 October the High Court noted that no compliance affidavit had been filed; the employees told it that a Supreme Court registry report showed the state's appeal was still defective, although the Chief Secretary had sworn that the defects had been cured. On 12 October the High Court issued a criminal contempt notice to the Chief Secretary and other officials.

## Why it matters

The case is being watched by government employees in other states where DA has fallen behind the central rate, including West Bengal, where the Supreme Court ruled in February that the state must pay its employees 25% of the DA arrears that built up between 2009 and 2019. The question running through these cases is whether a state can defer DA it has promised by pointing to its finances, and how far courts can go to enforce payment.

LiveLaw's report did not say how much Punjab owes or how many employees and pensioners are affected, and the Supreme Court's written order had not been published at the time of writing.

## What happens next

Punjab must tell the Supreme Court how much of the arrears it will clear by 31 March 2027. The appeals against the High Court judgment remain pending.
